chapter_theme: Pattinathar's first Koyil Thiruvagaval, one long unit addressed to the poet's own mind. Framed by the refrain 'think, mind, think of Siva of the golden hall', it argues from the reversibility of everything (what is born dies, what is eaten becomes excrement, what is loved becomes hated) and from the mind's own history across births, in which it has killed and been killed, eaten and been eaten, sat in heaven and lain in hell, to the body it has taken for stronger than stone, which is a hut of grass with openings for rheum, wax, mucus, spit, wind and urine and ends as burnt bone. Knowing this, the mind is to think of the Siva-bliss that stands beyond 'I' and 'mine', the two deeds, the malas, coming and going, night and day and this world and the next.
structure_note: Three movements inside the refrain: the pairs of reversal (பிறந்தன இறக்கும் ... உவப்பன வெறுப்பாம்), the mind's own career through births (கொன்றனை, தின்றனை, பெற்றனை, ஓம்பினை, each returned on it), and the anatomy of the body's openings, followed by the string of அற negatives that define the Lord and the closing call. The refrain stands at the head and the foot.

300.reading: Think, mind, of Siva of the golden hall and do not cherish the false life of the world or the body that staggers on the wheel of a demon's chariot: whatever is born dies and the dead are born, the large grows small and the small large, the known is forgotten and the forgotten known, what is eaten turns to excrement and what is adorned to dirt; through birth after birth you have killed all and all have killed you, eaten and been eaten, borne and been borne, rejoiced in wealth and wept in poverty, sat in heaven and lain in hell, and never once saw it as one; and this cage of the two deeds, a grass hut of a shelter with one opening for rheum, one for wax, one for mucus, one for spit and phlegm, one way for wind and excrement and one for urine and pus, stinking from within and ending as burnt bone, you took for firmer than stone. Knowing the bodily life from within, think of the god with konrai and matted hair, the unending Siva-bliss joined to you as a shadow that never leaves, free of 'I' and 'mine', of the two deeds and the malas, of coming and going, delusion and darkness, night and day, this world and the next, the First who rose as light in Tillai, the king of the hall, the dancer of bliss; melting like lac in fire, think of him, mind.
300.nuance: The argument is not that the world is unreal but that it is reversible: every pair runs both ways (பிறந்தன இறக்கும், இறந்தன பிறக்கும்), so nothing holds a state. The mind's career across births is told in a chiasmus, கொன்றனை அனைத்தும், அனைத்தும் நினைக் கொன்றன, which makes every act suffered as well as done; ஒன்றென்று எழியாது உற்றனை, that it never grasped all this as one, is the fault named. The body is counted by its openings, as in the Naladiyar and Tirumular's nine gates, and the stone the mind took it for returns in the Tirumanthiram as what the mind itself should become. அலகைத் தேரின் அலமரு காலின் is read as the staggering wheel of a demon's chariot; the simile is loose and some take அலகை as a kite or a mirage. நிழலெனக் கடவா நீர்மை, the nature that does not depart like a shadow, is the one positive description of the Lord's relation to the soul; everything else is said in அற, 'without'.

links.note: The Naladiyar's body is a pot that seeps filth from nine openings, called 'broad-shouldered one' by the fool; Pattinathar counts the openings one by one, rheum, wax, mucus, spit, wind and urine, and says the mind took this grass hut for firmer than stone. Both reduce the body to its leaks; the Naladiyar aims at the lover, Pattinathar at the mind's own trust in its body.

Tirumular says the mind made firm as stone stands before Siva while the body is brief as lightning; Pattinathar reproaches the mind for taking the body for firmer than stone (கல்லினும் வலிதாக் கருதினை). The same stone is misplaced in one and rightly placed in the other: the firmness belongs to the mind turned to Siva, not to the body.

The Kural says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' enters a world higher than the gods'; Pattinathar names the Siva-bliss as what stands free of 'I' and 'mine' (எனதற நினைவற) along with the two deeds and the malas. Both make the end of the two possessives the threshold; the Kural's reward is a higher world, Pattinathar's is the Lord himself.
